title: The peace to both sides
hook: turn right, then left: peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah

segments.voice: Yesterday: tashahhud, the testimony in the sitting, peace sent to every righteous servant. Your line was peace on us and the good. Did you send peace to someone you'll never meet? Day one hundred eight.
screen: `TASHAHHUD — PEACE ON US AND THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: How do you end a phone call with someone you love? Not just click. You say bye, and bye, and okay, bye, love you, bye. Endings matter. They tell the other person how you're leaving. Now, the prayer. The door closed behind you at the start, with Allahu akbar. For a few minutes you've been somewhere else: standing, bowing, on the floor, sitting. And now you have to come back into the room. How do you walk out of a conversation with God? Today: the peace to both sides.
screen: `OKAY, BYE, LOVE YOU, BYE.` → `ENDINGS MATTER.` → `HOW DO YOU WALK BACK OUT?`

segments.voice: The ending is called taslim, from the same root as salaam, the very first word on this path. In the most common form, at the end of the last sitting, the person turns the head to the right and says: as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah. Then to the left, and says it again. Remember the hadith from day one hundred one: the prayer's opening is the takbir, and its closing is the salam, the taslim. The door that closed with Allahu akbar opens again with peace. Who is the greeting for? The scholars give a few answers. The angels, whom the tradition places on the right and left of every person. The people praying beside you in the line. Muslims everywhere. The words are plural, you all, so there's room for all of them. There's a small story in Sahih Muslim that shows how ordinary it's meant to be. A companion named Jabir said that when they prayed with the Prophet ﷺ, they used to wave their hands at the salam, to one side and the other. The Prophet asked why they were waving like restless horses flicking their tails, and told them it was enough to rest the hand on the thigh and give the greeting to your brother on your right and on your left. Just turn your face, and wish peace to the person next to you. That's the last act of the prayer. It doesn't end with a request, or a flourish. It ends with you looking at the people beside you and wishing them peace and mercy.
screen: `TASLIM — FROM THE ROOT OF SALAAM.` · `RIGHT, THEN LEFT.` · `ITS CLOSING IS THE TASLIM.` · `NO NEED TO WAVE.` · then, large: `PEACE TO THE PERSON BESIDE YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn right and left. Sit comfortably, hands resting on your thighs. Take a breath. Turn your head slowly to the right, as far as is comfortable, and if you pray, say: as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah. If not, just think of whoever is on that side of you, in the next room, the next house, the next city, and wish them well. Then turn slowly to the left, and do the same. Come back to center, and sit. The bell holds the time.
Taslim. The closing of the prayer: peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah, turning right, then left. Today's word.
Your line: peace, both ways. The next time you leave a room, a call or a conversation today, leave it the way the prayer does: with a word of peace for whoever's there. Day one hundred eight.

howItsDone: Muslims end every prayer by turning the head to the right and then to the left, saying as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah each time, greeting the angels and the worshippers on either side.

options: rest your hand on your thigh and greet the person beside you

original.note: Arabic: peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah, said to the right and to the left.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims look over their shoulders at the end of prayer.
what it means: the taslim closes the prayer with a greeting of peace and mercy to both sides.
what a scholar hears: 'its closing is the taslim' (Abu Dawud 61); the plural 'alaykum; and Jabir's report of the waving hands (Muslim 431).

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 431 (Jabir: waving at the salam; greet the one on your right and left)
Sunan Abi Dawud 61; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3 (its closing is the taslim)
Qur'an 50:17 (the two receivers on the right and the left)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm.

Maliki practice commonly uses a single taslim to the front/right for one praying alone; Shia practice differs. The script gives the common two-sided form, now framed as 'the most common form', without spelling out these variants.
Before the taslim, the final sitting also includes the salawat on the Prophet and refuge-seeking; not covered here (salawat is day 119).
Who is greeted (angels, fellow worshippers) is a scholarly explanation, stated as such.
